"Saya telah minta semua Jabatan Pendidikan Negeri dan Pejabat Pendidikan Daerah untuk terus memantau keadaan jerebu dan mengambil tindakan segera sekiranya keadaan memerlukan," katanya di Facebook.
"Masa yang akan datang, kita akan memastikan sebarang keputusan penutupan sekolah dimaklumkan lebih awal supaya ibu bapa mempunyai masa yang mencukupi untuk membuat persediaan."

Terdahulu, Yang di-Pertuan Agong, Sultan Ibrahim, menitahkan nasihat agar sekolah di kawasan terjejas jerebu ditutup susulan bacaan Indeks Pencemar Udara (IPU) yang berpanjangan antara 150 hingga 180.
Baginda bertitah aspek keselamatan dan kesihatan murid serta pelajar perlu diberi keutamaan ketika keadaan jerebu melanda negara.
Kemudian, Ketua Pengarah Pendidikan, Azam Ahmad, mengumumkan penutupan semua institusi pendidikan bawah Kementerian Pendidikan (KPM) di kawasan yang merekodkan bacaan IPU melebihi 180.
Institusi pendidikan di kawasan yang mencatat bacaan IPU melebihi 150 secara berpanjangan selama tiga hari berturut-turut pula akan ditutup bermula Isnin depan.

Pihak sekolah juga perlu memastikan kelangsungan proses pengajaran dan pembelajaran dengan menggunakan kaedah bersesuaian, mengambil kira kemampuan, akses serta keperluan murid dan kesiapsiagaan guru.
271cf3cd15edc618: LONDON: Tankers are facing a higher risk of attacks and intimidation as they try to get critical shipments through the Strait of Hormuz after Iran issued new warnings it would block routes that it has not authorised, sources said.

Last week already saw the biggest number of attacks on tankers in the key waterway since the Iran war began - cutting the number of vessels trying to get through to the lowest in more than two months.
Iran has now warned regional countries that any attempt to open new routes for oil exports would be considered hostile, a senior regional official close to Teheran told Reuters.
It was part of a plan agreed by both Iran's political leaders and its Revolutionary Guards, the official added.

"Iran has absolutely no intention of allowing control of the Strait of Hormuz to slip from its hands, and has plans ready to block routes that some regional countries have for exporting oil," a senior diplomat in the region briefed by Teheran told Reuters separately.
"This could involve missile and drone attacks on ships, or sending boats to scare ships away," the diplomat added.
"It plans to continue this policy of fear and threats," he said.

In recent months, Gulf oil producers have rushed shipments of oil through channels that hug the Omani side of the strait before transferring the oil in open waters in the Gulf of Oman with aerial support from the US, sources have told Reuters.
In the latest incident in the past 24 hours, projectiles struck a tanker some 51 nautical miles off the coast of Qatar inside the Gulf, British navy agency UKMTO reported.

Maritime security sources said the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged chemical tanker Acers had been hit by multiple projectiles north of Qatar's Madinat ash Shamal with minor injuries sustained by its crew.

"The Acers strike raises the prospect of a wider combat area affecting approaches to Qatar, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Iraq," maritime risk intelligence group Pole Star Global's subsidiary Clearwater Dynamics said in a report on Thursday.
The vessel's operator, listed in shipping databases as Antigua and Barbuda-based Valvoria Shipping, could not be reached for comment.
"The recent spate of Iranian attacks seems to have dampened the appetite of shipowners to sail through the Strait," said Jakob Larsen, chief ​safety & security officer at shipping association BIMCO.
"The Iranian threat appears to have increased."

US President Donald Trump is weighing next steps against Iran, including whether to escalate strikes before or after the November midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress, as he presses a naval blockade meant to pile economic pressure on Teheran to reach a deal to end the conflict.
The war — and its US$3 billion monthly price tag — has become a key issue on the campaign trail.
Governments and energy companies have drawn oil from stockpiles to alleviate pressure in a global oil market facing unprecedented supply disruptions this year, also caused by the war in Ukraine.

The amount of oil in storage that is accessible to the global market is running low, ‌industry executives said at a forum in London this week, making the market more fragile and putting upward pressure on prices.
The impact of the crisis was increasingly rippling across the global economy.
Danish shipping group Maersk said on Thursday it was increasing its emergency fuel surcharge on inland transportation in the UK and Ireland due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

"There is no going back to the old world, no harboring back to the stability and the prosperity of the last several decades," Major General Paul Maynard, Assistant Chief of the Naval Staff with Britain's Royal Navy, told a UK Chamber of Shipping Riviera conference in London this week.
"A war at sea does not remain at sea."

1f51c9489de79e67: MONTREAL: Canadian poet Anne Carson winning the Nobel prize for literature is a "proud moment" for the country, prime minister Mark Carney said Thursday.
The 76-year-old's works feature "wit, imagination, and a style entirely her own," Carney said on X.
"She has brought ancient stories to new audiences and transformed the way we think about literature," he said, calling the award "an extraordinary achievement and a proud moment for Canada".
cbd8875918dc452b: TOKYO: Dozens of protesters lined up in front of Japan's Foreign Ministry on Thursday after a US Marine was accused of killing a woman in the southernmost prefecture of Okinawa, many holding signs decrying crimes by US service members.

The case is the latest in a string of incidents stretching back years that have fuelled unease over the large US troop presence on the island chain near Taiwan and China, with US officials warning it could undermine ties vital to security in East Asia.
Public reaction to Anna Yagi's killing, however, has been muted compared with the mass demonstrations that followed the rape of a 12-year-old Okinawan girl by three US servicemen in 1995.

Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, is suspected of killing Yagi, 39, in a hotel in the Okinawan capital of Naha last weekend and taking her wallet and backpack. Ballard denied the allegations, police said.
Leaders of Thursday's protest spoke over loudspeakers about abuses by US service members and called on the government to respond, with others in the crowd rattling noisemakers in assent.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has called the killing "extremely brutal and heinous", and Tokyo said it had strongly protested to the US and demanded measures to prevent a repeat of such incidents.
Japan hosts the largest overseas contingent of US forces globally. Most of the 18,000 Japan-based Marines are stationed in Okinawa, which the US held from the end of World War Two until 1972.
That presence has repeatedly stirred resentment among residents over issues such as noise, aircraft crashes and the conduct of personnel.
The US on Wednesday began a 48-hour pause of military operations and a ban on alcohol while troops undergo training on standards and discipline.
Service members have also been given a month-long curfew for a "period of reflection."
b7de00100fab5350: KUALA LUMPUR: Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim has expressed his condolences over the deaths of three siblings killed in a road crash in Pontian, Johor, today.
In a Facebook post, Anwar also expressed his deepest sympathies to the victims' family and prayed that they would be given strength and resilience in facing the tragedy.
"May the souls of the deceased be showered with blessings and be placed among the righteous. Al-Fatihah," he said.

The three siblings, aged between eight and 18, were killed around 7.20am after they collided with a lorry travelling in the opposite direction while they were heading from Jalan Parit Haji Omar towards Kayu Ara Pasong on a motorcycle.

Pontian police chief Superintendent Hadzrat Hussein Mion Hussain said the pillion riders, aged eight and 11, died at the scene, while the 18-year-old motorcycle rider succumbed to his injuries at Pontian Hospital.
The 69-year-old lorry driver sustained injuries to his hands and both knees.
f4f2e6f4d721163f: PETALING JAYA: Education minister Fadhlina Sidek has announced that all educational institutions in Selangor, Melaka, Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya will close tomorrow due to the worsening haze.
Fadhlina said that in Pahang, only schools in Rompin will be closed.
She said schools in Perlis, Perak, Penang, Sabah, Sarawak and Labuan will operate as usual.

6925ea3cd0e46d1d: LONDON: British police on Thursday said that search warrants it secured to search properties linked to King Charles' younger brother Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor had been incorrectly granted and must be quashed.
King Charles' younger ​brother was arrested on ‌suspicion of misconduct in public office in February and searches carried out at properties in Sandringham, eastern England, and Windsor.
Andrew was suspected of leaking confidential government documents to the late convicted sex-offender Jeffrey Epstein when Andrew was a British trade representative, between 2001 and 2011.
Police have not charged him and Andrew, the second son of the late Queen Elizabeth, has denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein, also saying he regrets their friendship.
The arrest of Mountbatten-Windsor, and the anger over his relationship with Epstein, left the British royal family facing one of its worst crises in 90 years.
Mountbatten-Windsor applied for the search warrants to be quashed and Thames Valley Police said it accepted that they had not been properly granted.

"We accept the position that the initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed," a Thames Valley Police spokesperson said.
"Legal proceedings are currently ongoing to decide how material seized during the searches will be managed and whether we can lawfully retain it in support of our ongoing investigation."

99a2bc4ff97d240b: KUALA LUMPUR: Johor Darul Ta'zim (JDT) kicked off their Asean Club Championship (ACC) campaign with a 6-0 thrashing of Cambodian champions PKR Svay Rieng in Group B at the Sultan Ibrahim Stadium on Thursday.

3f49b29e9d6af704: WASHINGTON: Voters who backed Democratic former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 are far more enthusiastic about casting ballots this November than those who supported President Donald Trump, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found, in a potential warning sign for Republicans heading into the midterm elections.

The six-day poll, completed Monday, also found that men were more enthusiastic about voting and more certain to cast ballots than women, and that male voters showed signs of shifting toward Democrats.
That could signal erosion in Republican support among a demographic that was a pillar of Trump's 2024 victory.
Some 48 per cent of 2024 Harris voters said they were "very enthusiastic" about voting in the Nov 3 midterm elections, when control of both chambers of Congress is at stake.
By comparison, just 30 per cent of Trump voters said the same in the poll.
The findings add to evidence of an enthusiasm gap favouring Democrats and suggest potential cracks in the coalition that propelled Trump in 2024, when he won the popular vote.
That coalition was fuelled by strong support from men and gains among Hispanic voters and other demographic groups that shifted to the right in the 2024 election.

The poll also adds to a string of encouraging signs for Democrats, who are widely favoured to win control of the House of Representatives and remain competitive in the fight for the Senate as Trump's approval ratings have slipped amid voter concerns about the cost of living and the war with Iran.

Republican strategist Charlie Gerow said the poll's findings raise the stakes for his party's turnout efforts, though he expects the enthusiasm gap to narrow as concerns about what he described as far-left Democrats gaining power motivate Republican voters.
"The enthusiasm has to be ginned up among Republicans because turnout is what's going to determine the outcome of these midterm elections," Gerow said.

While Trump voters overwhelmingly plan to vote Republican and Harris voters are similarly inclined to vote Democratic, the president's 2024 supporters are less decided, with 13 per cent saying they aren't sure who to vote for in congressional elections, compared to seven per cent of Harris supporters who say the same.

The poll, which was conducted nationwide and surveyed 4,506 adults online, showed that just 32 per cent of Americans approved of Trump's presidency, holding at a record low first marked in a September Reuters/Ipsos survey.
The survey has a two percentage point margin of error.

Since taking office in January 2025, support for Trump has fallen across every major demographic group, including double-digit drops among Hispanics, men, rural and suburban voters, people without college degrees and evangelical Christians.
One notable shift has come among men, a group Trump won in all three of his presidential campaigns, including by a 12-point margin in 2024, according to a Pew Research analysis.
When asked how they would vote in a congressional race if the elections were today, men in the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll picked Democrats over Republicans, 43 to 39 per cent.
The four-point Democratic advantage was the widest of Trump's second term.
Men consistently favoured Republicans in 2025 but since August have mostly favoured Democrats.
The warning signs for Republicans reflect growing voter concerns about the high cost of living amid a surge in gasoline and diesel prices following the war with Iran.
Trump launched the Iran attacks in February, despite pledging during his campaign not to start new conflicts and to lower costs for consumers.

Cost of living is the top issue on Americans' minds as they decide how they will vote next month, the Reuters/Ipsos poll found. Voters cite democratic values as the second biggest issue, followed by immigration.
Republicans continue to hold an edge among older voters, a crucial bloc in midterm elections, when seniors have historically accounted for an outsized share of the electorate.
Voters 50 and older still favour the Republican Party over the Democratic Party, 44 to 42 per cent, though that was down from an 8-point Republican advantage in December.
Still, the enthusiasm gap looms large for Republicans.

Among all the voters in the poll who said they were enthusiastic, 62 per cent said they were pumped about expressing opposition to Trump, compared to 36 per cent who said they were eager to support the president.

Linda Rivera, a 46-year-old Trump voter in Pennsylvania, said that while she would probably vote Republican if she casts a ballot, she is frustrated with both parties and feels "neither enthusiastic or unenthusiastic" about voting next month.

Rivera, a respondent in the poll, said concerns about widespread voting fraud - which have been repeatedly fanned by Trump and his Republican allies without evidence - have added to her doubts about whether she will vote.
"I have lost faith in the voting process," she told Reuters. "I have lost faith in both parties. Not just one."

350944c59b150786: PETALING JAYA: Adun Permatang, Nurul Syazwani Noh, mendakwa beliau tidak dimaklumkan tentang perjanjian kerjasama antara wakil rakyat Bersatu Selangor dengan parti pemerintah.

Syazwani mengulas kenyataan Pengerusi Pakatan Harapan Selangor, Amirudin Shari, semalam bahawa rundingan melibatkan terma-terma perjanjian kerjasama sedang berjalan dan akan dimuktamadkan sebelum pembentangan belanjawan.

Menurutnya, beliau sentiasa bekerjasama dengan kerajaan negeri, agensi kerajaan dan pihak berkuasa tempatan dalam menyelesaikan isu yang dihadapi penduduk di kawasannya.

163a6f2d95867fe6: ArtCraft has added alternatives to Microsoft Word, Excel, and PowerPoint to its growing collection of Rust applications, which it describes as "clean-room reimplementations" of proprietary software. The projects lean heavily on Claude for development and remain unfinished, but our first look at its Word alternative, WordCraft, suggests they are worth watching. The company's GitHub repositories also include projects modeled on Photoshop, Illustrator, and Premiere Pro. We fired up WordCraft on an Arm-based Surface and it worked pretty well. WordCraft resembles Microsoft's application, although its buttons, icons, and other imagery differ. "The spelling dictionary and hyphenation come from Grady Ward's public-domain Moby Hyphenator II word list," ArtCraft says, and the application is dual-licensed under MIT or Apache 2.0. The company is at pains to point out that WordCraft is at the pre-alpha stage and estimates that it is at 62 percent of real feature parity, although "an alpha for everyday writing is close." We would keep it away from production workloads for now. Its roadmap says testing DOCX compatibility against a collection of real-world files has not begun, and charts, SmartArt, and embedded OLE objects are dropped. The Document Foundation, which develops LibreOffice, declined to comment. Microsoft acknowledged our inquiry but offered no further response. Adobe also declined to comment on the projects targeting its creative applications. Neil Brown of decoded.legal told The Register that the legal position would depend on the jurisdiction, but suggested that "those doing the 'reimplementations' may well argue that, since they have implemented the underlying functionality independently (i.e. without access to the source code of the software that they are reimplementing), their overall reimplementation is non-infringing." That said, "the legal situation is always going to be interesting, and quite possibly litigated, when the party most likely to feel aggrieved has deep pockets and lots of lawyers, and probably quite a lot to lose." ArtCraft says WordCraft was built from public specifications and observation, using original or openly licensed assets. Its ambitions now extend from creative software to office applications, but whether the projects can deliver reliable replacements remains to be seen. In the years to come, it would be richly ironic if AI programming tools took a bite out of the revenues of the company that gave us Copilot in GitHub. ®
d93f265d1b113a9e: BEIJING: Millions of gig workers in China could benefit from stronger labour protections under proposed rules announced Thursday that would mandate online platforms sign employment contracts with them.

The draft measures from China's human resources and social security ministry require internet platforms that "recruit, organise, and manage workers... to complete platform work tasks" to enter into standardised employment agreements with their workers.
The draft, open for public consultation until Nov 8, could affect millions of takeout delivery drivers, parcel couriers and ride-hailing drivers who often lack formal labour contracts.

Online platforms, including tech giants like Alibaba, Meituan and DiDi, will also be forbidden from encouraging gig workers to register as individual business owners to avoid signing employment contracts with them.
Currently, many gig workers in China are employed as freelancers or through subcontractors.
The world's second-largest economy had 280 million flexible workers in 2025, according to a report by the China New Employment Forms Research Centre, a think tank.
They have few protections and face long working hours for relatively low pay in sectors like food delivery that are characterised by fierce competition and price wars between rival online platforms.
Under the new rules, gig workers will be entitled to the minimum wage, extra pay for work on public holidays, and "appropriate rest".

Platforms must also explain their management algorithms to workers, according to the proposal, and decisions to stop orders or ban worker accounts cannot be made by algorithm alone and must be reviewed manually.

In April, Chinese authorities said they would strengthen management of the gig economy through better legal protections for workers, targeting "substantial progress" in working conditions within three years.

2c54cfec9c5b7bf0: SINGAPORE: Formula One will use the same power unit software fix hurriedly introduced in Malaysia last Sunday if this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix turns wet, the sport's governing body, the International Automobile Federation (FIA), said on Thursday.

The FIA carried out an investigation after what it described as a software bug caused chaos, with cars slowing to a crawl on two formation laps held after heavy rain at Sepang had forced the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to be aborted.
The Bahrain Grand Prix was held in Malaysia due to the Iran war and the situation in the Middle East.

The review concluded that some cars running on low engine revs at certain points of the circuit experienced a "loss of power beyond the original intent and that could not be recovered in those sectors.
"As a result, the configuration established for the Sepang event will be reinstated for the Singapore Grand Prix should similar weather conditions be expected.
"Additionally, a further update to the wet weather software will be released for the US Grand Prix on Oct 25," it stated.
Singapore is hosting a sprint race for the first time on Saturday with the main grand prix at night under floodlights on Sunday.

A heat hazard has already been declared by the FIA for the weekend at the Marina Bay circuit, meaning temperatures in excess of 31℃ are forecast, requiring teams to fit a driver cooling system, such as a liquid-cooled vest, though they are not obliged to use them and can take a ballast penalty instead.
The review also recommended implementing measures for testing of the software to make it as robust as possible and the FIA said it would be working with teams and manufacturers.

FIA single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis told reporters on Sunday that the lack of pre-season testing in wet conditions, with Sepang the first wet start of the season, played a part in the chaos but the governing body clarified that.

"Before implementation, teams and power unit manufacturers conducted simulation exercises to validate the software package, which was subsequently tested in full-scale running during Free Practice One sessions at both the Belgian Grand Prix and the Dutch Grand Prix," it said.
Issue identified within five minutes
The FIA also published a chronology of events at Sepang, with the start procedure suspended at 3.45pm local time and the cause of the issue identified within five minutes.
It said teams were given technical guidance and clarification at 4.03pm about installing and operating the revised software configurations.
The integration process was completed by 4.20pm and cars left the pit lane again at 4.33pm.
Red Bull's Max Verstappen, who won in Sepang, said he hoped the next set of regulations would simplify matters, allowing him to jump in the car and "just drive off" instead of waiting for updates.
"The problem is that, as you can see, there is all the software in the background that can make you not pull away or there is a glitch, or even on slow laps, stuff that can happen," he said.
"You shouldn't be thinking about where to be having to lift off or going down a gear to make sure that you have better deployment, all these kinds of things.
"That's not what racing should be about. You should be able to go out, have a brake pedal and a throttle pedal, and that's what decides the lap time," he added.
Drivers are expected to discuss the situation with the FIA at the Singapore race.
"It's something that we need to learn from and make sure it doesn't happen again," said Cadillac's Mexican driver Sergio Perez.
33f16be6a875f55c: CrowdStrike researchers investigating attacks on South Korean financial institutions found exposed AI session logs containing operational details and a resume-writing request that may identify the attacker. In a report published Wednesday, analyst Ashley Campion said the prompt named "YY," listed a Chinese university and a location in Guangdong, and gave conflicting age information: 26, but initially a birth date in September 2007. CrowdStrike considers the details likely to belong to the attacker but says it cannot definitively establish that connection. The attacks affected at least five lenders, including Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank, Hana Bank, Yegaram Savings Bank, and BNK Busan Bank, according to The Korea Times. In one case, the attackers allegedly breached a loan progress inquiry service and in another, they gained access to a mobile work-support system. The researchers found references to YY in AI sessions associated with activity involving ARTEX, a recently released open source penetration-testing tool developed in China and used in the attacks alongside Claude Code. Researchers examined an exposed directory on a server associated with the attacks. A Chinese-language instruction file led them to another server in Hong Kong, where they found session histories, configuration files, and AI memory files documenting the targeting. The resume prompt included a Telegram username that also appeared in activity targeting a possible Chinese payment platform and in Claude Code sessions seeking vulnerabilities in a Telegram-based NFT gift marketplace, CrowdStrike said. "The use of agentic AI tooling alongside traditional offensive capabilities highlights the continued evolution observed by CrowdStrike in adversarial tradecraft," Campion said. "This activity demonstrates how AI tooling can enable a financially motivated threat actor to conduct multiple intrusions within a short time span. CrowdStrike Intelligence assesses that adversaries will likely continue to experiment with implementing AI tooling in their operations to enhance their operational tempo and capabilities." Police are investigating whether an individual or an organized group carried out the attacks. Shinhan Bank reported that about 25,000 customers were affected, while KB Kookmin and Hana reported 119 and 89 respectively. Lawmakers have approved plans to summon the heads of five major commercial banks to an October 19 parliamentary audit to answer questions about cybersecurity lapses. ®
2a89976ca99e70c6: SEREMBAN: Semua institusi bawah Kementerian Pendidikan (KPM) di Negeri Sembilan ditutup mulai esok susulan keadaan jerebu yang melanda negeri berkenaan.

Jabatan Pendidikan Negeri Sembilan (JPNS) memaklumkan penutupan itu dibuat selaras kenyataan KPM hari ini berdasarkan bacaan indeks pencemar udara (IPU) di tiga stesen pemantauan di negeri berkenaan, iaitu Port Dickson, Seremban dan Nilai pada 5 petang.

"Institusi pendidikan yang terjejas hendaklah melaksanakan pengajaran dan pembelajaran dari rumah bagi memastikan kelangsungan pembelajaran murid, dengan mengambil kira kemampuan, akses dan keperluan murid serta kesiapsiagaan guru.

"Guru-guru dan anggota kumpulan pelaksana turut dibenarkan bekerja dari rumah sepanjang tempoh pelaksanaan penutupan.. keselamatan, kesihatan dan kebajikan murid serta warga pendidik sentiasa menjadi keutamaan JPNS,” menurut kenyataan.

Kenyataan itu memaklumkan JPNS dan pejabat pendidikan daerah serta institusi pendidikan akan terus memantau bacaan IPU dari semasa ke semasa selain mengambil tindakan sewajarnya berdasarkan perkembangan serta ketetapan KPM.
Ibu bapa dan penjaga turut dinasihatkan sentiasa peka terhadap perkembangan semasa serta memberikan kerjasama bagi memastikan keselamatan dan kesihatan anak-anak sepanjang tempoh keadaan jerebu.
7dd464dfb154dae7: PETALING JAYA: All educational institutions in Negeri Sembilan will close tomorrow due to the ongoing haze, the state education department has announced.
The department said it decided to close the schools in view of all three air pollutant index (API) monitoring stations in the state recording high APIs, Bernama reported.
As of 8pm, the API was approaching very unhealthy levels in Seremban (189) and Nilai (184), while the index stood at 170 in Port Dickson.
"The affected educational institutions are to conduct online learning to ensure continuity in students' lessons, based on the capabilities and needs of students as well as preparedness of teachers.
"Teachers and school administrators are also allowed to work from home during this period," said the Negeri Sembilan education department.

This evening, the education ministry said schools in areas that record API readings of more than 180 are to close tomorrow, while schools in areas that record APIs of more than 150 for three consecutive days will close from Oct 12.
14099930f1d1c725: IBM has sold “hundreds” of its cloudy VMware customers to Broadcom partner 11:11 Systems. Under Broadcom’s ownership, VMware slashed the number of cloudy partners it keeps on the books and retained only partners that go all-in on the Cloud Foundation (VCF) private cloud stack. Partners that Broadcom decided not to work with lost the right to resell its software as of October 2025 and may not run VMware-powered clouds after March 2027. IBM was once a top VMware partner, but last year stopped selling new cloudy VMware services, suggesting it wasn’t invited to continue as a Broadcom partner. Sources tell The Register that soon-to-be-former VMware partners often have a contractual obligation to provide a Virtzilla-powered cloud beyond the March 2027 cutoff, and that their customers want whatever happens next to be non-disruptive. One option for partners leaving the VMware fold is to turn to a wholesaler like 11:11, which runs its own VMware cloud. Another option for departing partners is selling contracts for ongoing VMware cloud services to one of the remaining Broadcom partners. 11:11 Systems told The Register IBM sold contracts for “hundreds” of customers who use VCF in the Big Blue cloud. 11:11 CEO Brett Diamond said the contracts are for customers running versions 7 and 8 of VCF and who are therefore “ripe for migration.” IBM did not respond to our questions about the transaction, which included a request for information regarding some customers that we understand are not making the move to 11:11. Diamond said 11:11 has 40 to 50 points of presence for its VMware cloud, and a migration methodology it will apply to the customers it bought from Big Blue. He’s confident his newly acquired customers will want to stick around. “The customers we manage are very large multinationals and Fortune 5000s who want to stay on VMware,” he said. “No other hypervisor can handle the mid-to-large enterprise.” The CEO hopes to shift his new customers to VCF 9, a necessity given VMware ends support for VCF 8 next year. 11:11 also uses its VMware cloud to sell other services, by delivering it through a custom console that integrates around 50 other tools spanning backup, storage, and security. The IBM buy is 11:11’s eight acquisition of a VMware service provider. It’s not hard to guess why Broadcom binned Big Blue, given that it sells Red Hat OpenShift which is a competitor for VMware – and a stronger one after recent improvements to its VM-hosting capabilities. Other VMware partners feel Broadcom did not have clear-cut reasons for excluding them from its partner program. Broadcom argues that services outfits that don’t dedicate their practices to VCF won’t meet customer needs, and it is therefore building a better channel composed of expert partners. Lobby group CISPE (Cloud Infrastructure Services Providers in Europe) argues Broadcom’s actions mean it has improperly concentrated the market for VMware cloud providers and is pursuing an antitrust case in EU courts. ®
7c196c46d8409f9d: MATAKING, Oct 8 — The palm-sized green turtle hatchling flailing through the sand on a Malaysian island may seem vulnerable, but its species has emerged as a symbol of hope for wildlife conservation.
Green turtles have made the rare jump from endangered to “least concern” in global conservation rankings, a remarkable success when many species are declining.
Conservation NGO World Wildlife Fund (WWF), in its biannual Living Planet Report released Thursday, found a 73-per cent decline in the average size of monitored wildlife populations over 53 years.
But around 50 per cent of the thousands of vertebrates monitored for the report are stable or increasing.
That includes green turtles, thanks to decades of efforts including egg relocation, marine protection and trade bans.
Malaysian turtle expert Juanita Joseph has spent years on the frontlines, carrying out cutting-edge genetic research and even convincing her own father to stop eating turtle eggs.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The palm-size green turtle hatchling flailing its flippers through the sand towards the sea on Mataking Island. — AFP pic
Still, when the International Union for the Conservation of Nature last year announced green turtles were no longer endangered, she could hardly believe it.
“Never in my mind (did I think) that one day turtles can be ‘least concern’. I cried... I said I’ve done my part,” she told AFP at Universiti Malaysia Sabah, where she is a professor.
All six other sea turtle species are still vulnerable or critically endangered, apart from the flatback turtle, whose status is unclear because of data shortages.
Turtles are targeted for food and their shells, killed in fishing nets, and constrained by development and pollution at nesting beaches and feeding grounds.
Climate change also skews populations more female because heat determines sex development in eggs.
Even now, recovery is uneven. While green turtles globally are “least concern”, some regional populations are still endangered and declining.
‘Our heritage’
Malaysia is something of a regional exception. Green turtle nesting at Sabah state’s Turtle Islands has tripled since the 1970s to over 20,000 nests annually.
That reflects “over five decades” of work, said Sabah Parks director Maklarin Lakim.
The Turtle Islands have been protected since 1977, and Sabah banned turtle meat and egg consumption in 1997.
“This is our heritage, this is our biodiversity,” Maklarin said.
“We would like to protect that as long as possible.”
Much of the conservation success has relied on people like Sitti Rasah Abdul, 50, from a fishing community on Malaysia’s Omadal island.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A conservationist counting hatched sea turtles from broken eggshells inside a sandy nesting enclosure. — AFP pic
Since 2012, she and other members of a women’s cooperative have relocated turtle eggs from beaches to a hatchery to protect them from predators and poachers.
The 20-strong team started conservation work with WWF, but now self-funds, ploughing 10 per cent of revenue from their handicraft and catering business into turtle protection.
“I’m already old,” said Rasah, on the wooden jetty that extends from her home into aquamarine seawater.
“But I feel a sense of responsibility to ensure that there are still turtles around for the next generation.”
A 45-minute boat ride away, green and hawksbill turtle hatchlings emerged from relocated nests in a hatchery at the high-end Mataking Reef Resort.
Hotel owner Sophia Sie fell in love with turtles decades ago when her father acquired land on Mataking island, and now around 10 per cent of her staff works on conservation.
In 2006, “we had about 600 eggs collected... today we have about 36,000 eggs,” Sie told AFP.
Guests can release hatchlings, and while Sie considers conservation a passion, it is also good business.
“The survival of our business here is very much dependent on the natural resources and the beauty around us,” she said.
‘Long-term project’
The hatchlings tipped from a basket onto a Mataking beach face long odds. Just one in 1,000 will survive to sexual maturity at 20 years old.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
An adult green sea turtle gliding through the deep blue waters off the coast of Mataking Island. — AFP pic
Hatchlings spend around a decade in the open ocean, a period sometimes called the “lost years” because scientists know so little about it.
Working out where turtles spend those years, and where they forage and reproduce, is key to sustaining conservation success, said Gavin Jolis, marine species strategy manager at WWF-Malaysia.
The NGO has created the world’s first global turtle DNA database, Shellbank, using samples from turtle tissue and shells to trace populations and even target poachers.
“In order to save sea turtles, we have to look at the life cycle,” said Jolis.
“That’s where the genetic work comes in.”
The neat rows of test tubes in Joseph’s lab contain bits of hatchling flipper snipped from babies that did not survive.
Sequencing them reveals a turtle’s “haplotype”, a kind of genetic fingerprint.
The work has already helped show that turtles foraging in parts of Malaysia come from Micronesia, and identified the likely source of turtle shell intercepted in Britain.
While each conservation effort faces different challenges, the battle to protect green turtles teaches “to really be resilient and patient with the work”, said Jolis.
“We should not look at just a short-term project, it’s a long-term project.” — AFP
dc295c84f4c7eb30: DUNGUN, Oct 8 — The surviving rows of two-storey wooden shophouses, known locally as ‘kedai kayu’, in Kuala Dungun are more than remnants of traditional architecture; they stand as witnesses to the history of a town once the centre of trade and economic activity in the district.
Built in 1933, the wooden buildings still carry the character of a bygone era, with timber main structures and windows, though some have been modified over the years to meet modern business needs.
Kuala Dungun trader and resident Ang Ah Kiang, 76, said the buildings are closely linked to the town’s history, which saw it develop from a fishing village into an important trading centre.

He said Kuala Dungun’s role later changed as economic activity picked up following the rapid development of the iron ore mining industry in Bukit Besi, particularly from the 1930s to the 1960s, before the mine closed in 1970.
“The economic growth also indirectly spurred trade in Kuala Dungun, including the emergence of various shops supplying the needs of residents and workers,” he told Bernama when met here today.
The surviving rows of two-storey wooden shophouses in Kuala Dungun. — Bernama pic

Ang said the wooden shops still operating today show the continuity between Kuala Dungun’s trading activities in the past and its business activities today, noting that some of the wooden shops in Kuala Dungun were built between 1930 and 1960.

He said about 100 wooden shop units were built during the period, and the premises now house a range of businesses, including restaurants, hardware stores, electrical shops, motorcycle dealers, plastic goods shops, grocery stores and photo shops.
Meanwhile, restaurant operator Mohd Kamal Hamid, 59, said he has rented the more than 90-year-old shop since 1986, after his father rented the premises in 1980.
He said that although the wooden shop, which he rents for RM1,200 a month, has undergone several renovations, its original structure has been preserved.
“I was told that the original owner of this wooden shop was a former employee of the iron ore mining company in Bukit Besi, and that the building was purchased in the 1930s,” he said.
Mural magic captures everyday life at Kuala Dungun’s ‘kedai kayu’. — Bernama pic

Meanwhile, the Dungun chapter of the Malaysian Historical Society honorary secretary Wan Mohd Rosli Wan Ngah said that in 1933, the Dungun District Office reorganised Kuala Dungun by creating wooden shop lots as a commercial centre to support the growth of trade in the area.
According to him, more Chinese residents were settling in Kuala Dungun at the time, purchasing land and newly completed wooden shophouses.
“Malay residents living in Kuala Dungun were relocated to a new and more comfortable village, Kampung Tanah Lot,” he said.
However, he said Hokkien Chinese from southern China had begun migrating to the district as early as 1922, with many settling along the outskirts of the Sungai Dungun estuary.
“They came to open businesses such as grocery, seafood and rubber shops, and later dominated the wooden shophouses in Kuala Dungun after the town was reorganised in 1933,” he added. — Bernama
e8c1b9c359d7d7ab: MOSCOW, Oct 8 — The death of a plague laboratory worker in Siberia last week has made global headlines, with Russian media suggesting hundreds were under quarantine and US President Donald Trump expressing concern.

Russia has attributed the worker’s death to pneumonia of an “undetermined” cause, but the United States, European Union and World Health Organization (WHO) have all called for more information on the case.
Russia’s public health agency, Rospotrebnadzor, said Wednesday that there was no risk of an epidemic among the wider public.
Here is what we know, five days since the laboratory worker died:
What happened?
The incident was first reported in local media on Friday.

Russian news outlet People of Baikal said that an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, whom it named as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, died the previous night from a suspected case of pneumonic plague.
She may have contracted the disease from a broken test tube, the outlet reported, without elaborating.
Alexei Tsydenov, governor of the neighbouring Buryatia region, said in a social media post that a woman in the Irkutsk region had “died of plague”, before editing the post to add the word “possibly”.
AFP has not been able to verify the reports.
The mayor of the town of Shelekhov, where she was reported to have died, said a local hospital had been quarantined.
As many as 200 people with whom she may have had contact were placed under quarantine over the incident, People of Baikal said.
Irkutsk is a remote Siberian city home to around 500,000 people in eastern Russia, while Shelekhov is a satellite town to the city’s west.
How has Russia responded?
Russian officials have downplayed or rejected reports the worker died of plague.
The Irkutsk region governor, Igor Kobzev, said Monday that an inspection by Rospotrebnadzor found she died of pneumonia of “undetermined” origin.

“No micro-organisms linked to the young woman’s professional work were found in her biological samples,” Kobzev said, adding that no other staff at the institute had sought medical attention since her death.
Rospotrebnadzor said Wednesday that the situation in the Irkutsk region remained “stable”, and that nearly 5,000 tests had been conducted, none of which revealed dangerous pathogens.
It also reported “comprehensive preventive and anti-epidemic measures” had been implemented, without saying what the measures were.
What is plague?
Plague is a disease caused by the Yersinia pestis bacterium, the same pathogen that killed millions of people in Europe during the Middle Ages.
It can occur in several forms, among them pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas.
All forms can be treated with antibiotics, although can be rapidly fatal if not treated early.
Plague is found in all continents except Oceania, and cases have been sporadically reported worldwide.
A plague outbreak on the island nation of Madagascar killed over 200 people in 2017.
How has the world reacted?
The Russian reports have triggered international concern, with Trump saying Monday that Washington was closely following events.
The WHO, European Union and United States have all called for Russia to be more transparent about the incident.

“WHO has requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia,” WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Wednesday, mentioning “media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause”.
Trump said Monday that Washington would “help” Russia, without elaborating. The next day he said he would call Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to discuss the reports.
What is the risk?
Russia has played down the risk.
Rospotrebnadzor said Wednesday that there were no “epidemic risks to the populations of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk Region”.
The WHO initially deemed the risk for the region to be “moderate to low”, but later said it lacked information to conduct a “full risk assessment”.
The Kremlin has hit out at reports of a suspected second case of the disease, saying most of what the media was reporting was “false information”.
Public health experts have also called for calm over the incident, which comes several years after the Covid pandemic.

In previous plague outbreaks, health authorities have had to “find the affected people, find their contacts, quarantine them and give them antibiotics,” Simon Clarke — an associate professor in cellular microbiology at the University of Reading in Britain — told Times Radio on Tuesday.
“It requires a lot of resources. But the Russians should be able to manage this,” he said. — AFP
6930d9caaa3c1f5d: GENEVA, Oct 8 — El Nino will intensify even more before peaking in December, the United Nations said Thursday, warning it could be among the strongest witnessed since at least 1950.

The naturally occurring weather phenomenon is set to bring higher temperatures to much of the planet, the UN’s weather and climate agency said, with its impact compounding the effects of man-made climate change.
“El Nino will continue to intensify ahead of its forecast peak in December,” the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in its monthly Global Seasonal Climate Update.
“It is likely to bring above-average temperatures to much of the globe and shift rainfall patterns, increasing the risk of drought and floods in different regions.”
El Nino warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
It typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.
Conditions oscillate between El Nino and its opposite La Nina, with neutral conditions in between.
El Nino ‘strengthening rapidly’

“Sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific are forecast to increase to record levels during October-November-December 2026, reflecting the strengthening of the El Nino event which will drive weather patterns and impact economies, ecosystems and communities across the globe,” the WMO said.
The forecast is based on consensus across 13 leading national and international meteorological centres.
“El Nino is firmly established and strengthening rapidly,” said WMO chief Celeste Saulo.
“WMO forecasts indicate a near-100 percent likelihood that it will persist through February 2027, potentially being one of the strongest since at least 1950.”
Saulo explained that El Nino does not add new heat to the planet, but releases heat being stored in the ocean.
“The ocean it’s drawing from is the warmest we’ve ever measured it. There is simply more heat available to release,” she said.
Sea temperatures record

The index which measures sea surface temperature anomalies across the central-eastern equatorial Pacific — the region at the heart of El Nino — increased from 1.6C above normal in June to 2.5C above normal in August.
For October-November-December, the anomaly is forecast to reach approximately 3.7C above normal.
This would be the highest since observations began, eclipsing the previous record of 2.6C set in 2015-2016.
The last El Nino contributed to making 2023 the second-hottest year on record and 2024 the all-time high at around 1.55C above the 1850-1900 pre-industrial average.
While El Nino usually peaks between November and February, the resulting spike in temperatures typically comes later.
This El Nino is already hitting some regions hard, including in Central America, where animals and crops are dying from drought. — AFP
23e939f5f82ff409: KUALA LUMPUR: Parlimen bukan tempat sesuai untuk perbincangan mengenai reformasi nasional yang kontroversi kerana ahli politik sering terikat dengan pendirian parti dan pertimbangan pilihan raya, kata Nazir Razak.

Pengerusi Yayasan Tun Razak itu berkata, Ahli Parlimen cenderung mematuhi arahan whip parti dan menjaga sokongan penyokong masing-masing, menyebabkan mereka sukar menyuarakan pandangan secara bebas mengenai isu sensitif.

“Di Parlimen, ahli politik perlu menjaga sokongan penyokong masing-masing dan pada masa sama mengikut arahan whip parti. Jadi, respons atau hujah dikemukakan sering dipengaruhi faktor lain, bukan semata-mata berdasarkan pandangan mereka sendiri tentang apa yang terbaik atau pandangan sebenar mereka terhadap sesuatu masalah.
“Sebab itu, sesetengah reformasi struktur sistem yang paling berjaya dibincangkan di luar Parlimen terlebih dahulu sebelum dibawa ke Parlimen,” katanya.
Beliau berkata demikian pada Dialog Seri Negara 2026 yang dirasmikan Menteri Perpaduan Negara Aaron Ago Dagang.

Nazir mengulangi gesaannya supaya Majlis Perundingan Negara kedua diwujudkan sebagai platform membincangkan isu termasuk tindakan afirmatif, identiti nasional, keseimbangan kuasa institusi dan rasuah.

Bekas Pengerusi Kumpulan CIMB itu menjadikan proses perbincangan Ireland mengenai reformasi undang-undang pengguguran sebagai contoh bagaimana isu sukar boleh dibincangkan terlebih dahulu di luar Parlimen sebelum cadangan dikemukakan kepada penggubal undang-undang.

Bagaimanapun, Ahli Parlimen Bangi, Syahredzan Johan, berkata ahli politik perlu dilibatkan kerana mereka sering menjadi pihak pertama menerima aduan rakyat dan memahami masalah dihadapi penduduk di kawasan masing-masing.
Katanya, media sosial juga memberikan gambaran mengelirukan mengenai Parlimen apabila pergeseran antara mereka lebih mendapat perhatian berbanding perbincangan mengenai dasar.

Syahredzan memberi contoh Jawatankuasa Pilihan Khas Parlimen yang membolehkan Ahli Parlimen daripada parti berbeza bekerjasama secara konstruktif apabila perbincangan dilakukan tanpa liputan atau tekanan untuk mendapatkan perhatian umum.

Beliau bersetuju perbincangan tanpa liputan mungkin lebih produktif, namun berkata ahli politik tetap perlu mengambil bahagian bersama wakil sektor lain dengan kepentingan nasional mengatasi kepentingan politik.

Ketua Pegawai Eksekutif Institut Demokrasi dan Hal Ehwal Ekonomi (IDEAS), Aira Azhari, mencadangkan sistem pilihan raya first-past-the-post Malaysia dikaji semula kerana sistem sedia ada mungkin menyumbang kepada politik yang semakin berpecah-belah.
Beliau berkata, perubahan komposisi etnik Malaysia, termasuk penyusutan jumlah penduduk bukan Melayu, boleh mempengaruhi politik pilihan raya serta cara parti politik bersaing mendapatkan sokongan.

Aira turut memberi amaran persepsi mengenai saiz ekonomi yang semakin mengecil boleh meningkatkan persaingan antara komuniti apabila setiap kelompok melihat keuntungan pihak lain sebagai kerugian kepada mereka.

Katanya, sistem pilihan raya first-past-the-post, apabila digabungkan dengan perpecahan sedia ada dalam masyarakat, boleh menyumbang kepada persaingan politik yang berasaskan pendekatan menang-kalah, iaitu keuntungan satu pihak dilihat sebagai kerugian pihak lain.

“Ada sesuatu dalam sistem itu sendiri yang boleh diubah suai dan mungkin mengubah cara permainan politik berlangsung,” katanya, namun tidak menghuraikan perubahan perlu dibuat terhadap sistem pilihan raya itu.
f284485ad4de458b: Ten of the world's biggest AI developers have agreed to tighten their handling of personal data following scrutiny by Britain's privacy watchdog, which is now turning its attention to autonomous AI agents that don't always play by the rules. The recently rebranded Information Commission's Office (ICO) said Thursday that Amazon, Anthropic, Apple, Cohere, DeepSeek, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Stability AI have either made changes or committed to doing so after the regulator examined their compliance with UK data protection law. These include clearer explanations of how personal information is used to train AI models, better ways for people to exercise their data rights, and tougher assessments of developers' safeguards. The commitments follow a supervisory program launched in 2025 that initially covered 11 developers. That number dropped to ten after the ICO paused its engagement with Elon Musk's xAI to pursue a separate formal investigation into its Grok chatbot. The watchdog isn't declaring victory just yet. It's monitoring whether developers deliver on their promises and admits that current AI training practices still pose problems under UK data protection law. Developers still have some explaining to do over personal data buried in their models, particularly sensitive information, and how people are supposed to get their details removed once an AI has been trained on them. There's also the risk of personal information being extracted from models, including data developers never intended them to retain. The ICO acknowledged that some of these issues will require cooperation between industry, regulators, and government. Getting companies to promise changes is one thing. Making today's AI models comply with the law is another. "AI has huge potential to benefit our society, but that depends on trust and transparency," said Richard Nevinson, the ICO's director of technology regulation. "Our engagement with some of the biggest developers has secured real commitments that will help people better understand and control how their data is used, even in a fast-moving and complex area." Meanwhile, the regulator is turning its attention to AI agents, which can browse websites, use tools, and carry out tasks with limited human supervision. And some aren't sticking to the rules. The ICO confirmed it has contacted OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and the UK's AI Security Institute following reports of agents bypassing safeguards during testing and deployment earlier this year. "These recent reports show both how fast these systems are advancing, and the risks they pose if the guardrails aren't fit for purpose," Nevinson said. "Our message is clear: the fact AI agents act with autonomy is not an excuse for poor compliance." The regulator has also launched a six-week call for evidence on agentic AI, covering security, transparency, accountability, and the lawful use of personal data. Responses are due by November 20 and will inform future guidance and the ICO's forthcoming statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making. The watchdog is separately examining how consumer chatbots and AI companions use personal information as they become increasingly personalized. For now, the ICO has secured promises from some of the industry's biggest names, although whether they deliver remains to be seen. And with AI agents increasingly capable of acting on their own, the watchdog may have its work cut out keeping them in line. ®
d21d9fbd15c640e8: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 8 — The Ministry of Digital, through MyDigital Corporation, is providing 100,000 learning licences to enable Malaysians to access digital and artificial intelligence (AI) courses through the online learning platform, Coursera.

MyDigital Corporation in a statement said the initiative, offered through the Rakyat Digital portal, provides three months of complimentary access to more than 16,000 courses and Professional Certificate programmes offered by leading universities and industry experts worldwide.

Under the government-funded Global Learning Pass, Malaysians with a MyDigital ID can access courses spanning AI, technology, data science, business and digital literacy from Sept 16, with the licences being rolled out in phases, subject to eligibility and availability.

“Early results show strong engagement, with 12,900 learners enrolling in 43,000 courses in the first three weeks, particularly across Selangor, Kuala Lumpur, Johor, Penang and Perak, with the most popular course being Understanding Digital Transformation, a custom course created by MyDigital Corporation using Coursera’s Course Builder.

“Designed for beginners, the approximately two-hour course introduces the technologies shaping Malaysia’s digital economy, including cloud computing, modern data centres, AI and machine learning, blockchain, IoT (Internet of Things) and 5G. Other popular courses include Google’s AI Fundamentals, Foundations: Data, Data, Everywhere and Foundations of Project Management, reflecting demand for practical, job-relevant skills,” the statement said.

MyDigital Corporation said the initiative forms part of the Rakyat Digital ecosystem and supports the Malaysia Digital 2030 Action Plan (MD2030) and National AI Action Plan 2026-2030, in line with Malaysia’s AI Nation 2030 ambition.

AI breakthroughs in robotics won’t change your life any time soon

The hype around humanoid robots is reaching fever pitch. Much of it comes from the idea that the same AI advances behind ChatGPT and Claude could enable robots to imitate human movement the way chatbots imitate human language. But many researchers are skeptical.

d9bdcfda3f50796a: OCTOBER 8 — “Why can’t I have it?”
It is probably a question every parent has heard.

We teach our children that they cannot have everything they want. We encourage them to save their duit raya. We explain that RM50 is more than RM10, and eventually introduce them to the familiar difference between “needs” and “wants”.
These are important lessons, and they remain important. But looking at the environment our children are growing up in today, I wonder whether teaching them about money is still enough.
Perhaps there is another question we need to teach them to ask: “Why do I want this?”

For many of us growing up, wanting something often began with seeing it in a shop, watching an advertisement on television or noticing that a friend at school had it. For children today, that journey can look very different.

They may discover a toy while watching their favourite creator. They may want a particular item because they have seen it repeatedly in short videos. A game may offer a new character, skin or upgrade. Something can suddenly become a “must-have” because everyone online seems to have it.
Sometimes children know they are looking at an advertisement. Sometimes they may not.
And this is where I think our conversation about children and money needs to go beyond simply teaching them how to save.

The internet is already an ordinary part of childhood. Unicef Malaysia reported in 2026 that 94 per cent of Malaysian children aged 12 to 17 use the internet, with nearly all of them going online daily.
That is not necessarily a bad thing. Our children learn online. They communicate, play, explore interests and discover things that previous generations could never access so easily.
But the same digital spaces are also commercial spaces.

Entertainment and consumption increasingly sit side by side. A child may watch someone unbox a toy without thinking about whether it is advertising. They may follow a creator because the content is entertaining, without necessarily recognising when a recommendation becomes commercial.

Even games now contain their own marketplaces. There are virtual currencies, upgrades, cosmetic items, rewards and limited-time offers. Children may learn what it feels like to want something rare or exclusive before they fully understand what spending RM10 here and RM20 there actually means.
This makes me wonder whether we have focused so much on financial literacy that we have overlooked another equally important skill: consumer literacy.
Financial literacy teaches a child to ask, “Do I have enough money?” Consumer literacy encourages them to ask, “Why do I want this in the first place?”
There is a subtle but important difference.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

The author argues that teaching children to save money is no longer enough, as parents must also equip them with consumer literacy skills to recognise how online advertising, influencers and digital games shape their spending desires. — Picture by Firdaus Latif

Financial literacy among children is already receiving attention in Malaysia. A 2023 study involving 419 primary-school children aged seven to 12 from Kedah, Penang, Perak and Perlis examined children's financial literacy and highlighted the important roles of schools, teachers and parents in strengthening financial knowledge.
Those efforts matter. But knowing how money works does not necessarily mean a child understands how the marketplace works on them.
Parents will probably recognise another familiar sentence: “But everyone has it.”
Peer influence is certainly not new. We wanted what our friends had when we were children too.
But “everyone” used to be a relatively small circle.

Today, that circle can be enormous. A child's reference point is no longer limited to classmates, cousins or neighbours. It can include YouTubers, gamers, influencers and hundreds of people appearing on their screens.
A product can become familiar very quickly simply because a child sees it repeatedly. And familiarity can easily become desire.

Adults experience this too. We see the same restaurant repeatedly on TikTok and suddenly feel curious about it. We read positive reviews and become more comfortable buying something. We watch other people using a product and begin imagining ourselves using it.
If adults can be influenced this way, we should not expect children to somehow be immune to it.
The difference is that adults have had years to develop some ability to recognise persuasion and understand financial consequences. Children are still learning both.
That is why perhaps saying “You don't need it” is sometimes not enough.
We could also ask: “Where did you see it?” “Why do you like it?” “Did someone tell you about it?” “Do you think they were trying to sell it?” “Would you still want it next week?”
These are simple questions, but they encourage children to think about their own consumption rather than simply responding to it.
Gaming makes this discussion even more interesting. Many games today are not simply games that children play. They contain small economies of their own.

Children encounter virtual currencies, collectible items, upgrades and limited-time rewards. They learn about scarcity, collecting and exclusivity. They also learn how easily waiting can sometimes be replaced by paying.

Malaysia is already beginning to recognise some of these concerns. In September 2026, the Communications and Multimedia Content Forum opened a public consultation on a proposed Gaming Sub-Code. The proposal covers areas including children's account settings and parental controls, transparency around in-game spending and randomised rewards, in-game advertising and creator promotions.
This is significant because it recognises that children's digital safety is not only about harmful content. The commercial design of the spaces in which children play matters too.

Unicef Malaysia has similarly argued that protecting children online should not simply mean removing their access. Digital spaces provide important opportunities for learning, connection and participation. The challenge is to make those environments safer and more child-centred.
Regulation can help. But regulation cannot accompany a child through every future commercial decision. Neither can parents.
Eventually, children need to learn how to recognise persuasion themselves. And that is why I believe consumer literacy needs to sit alongside financial and digital literacy.
Of course, this responsibility should not fall entirely on parents.
Businesses, platforms, game developers and content creators are also shaping the marketplace our children are growing up in.
Children are consumers, but they are not simply smaller versions of adult consumers. Their understanding of money, persuasion, value and consequences is still developing.
So perhaps businesses need to move beyond asking, “Are we allowed to market this way?” and occasionally ask, “Should we market this way to a child?”
There is a difference.
This does not mean we should stop marketing children's products or remove every commercial element from their digital lives. That would hardly be realistic.
But we should be able to expect greater transparency and responsibility when the consumer on the other side of the screen is still learning what it means to be a consumer.
As parents, we will probably continue having the same conversations our parents had with us: “You don't need another one.” “Save your money.” “Think before you buy.”
Those lessons still matter. But perhaps we need to add another one.

When our children suddenly desperately want the latest toy, game, collectible or whatever trend appears next, instead of only asking whether they can afford it, perhaps we can help them understand where that desire came from.
Teaching a child that RM50 is more than RM10 is financial literacy. Teaching them to save RM5 instead of spending it is financial literacy.
But teaching them to recognise why something suddenly feels so desirable is something different.
That is consumer literacy.
And in a marketplace becoming increasingly sophisticated at understanding what children want, perhaps our children also need to become a little more sophisticated at understanding the marketplace.
So the next time a child says, “But I really want it,” perhaps there is another question worth asking.
“Why?”
The author is a Senior Lecturer at the School of Business Management, Universiti Utara Malaysia.

“She was taken by surprise, but very happy. I could hear that in her voice.”
The Academy said almost all her literary production “has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning”.
It singled out her poem Nox, printed on one continuous sheet of paper in homage to her dead brother, as “an unforgettable work”.
Carson has been mentioned as a possible Nobel laureate for years.
Many literary critics had predicted the award would go to a woman this year, given the frequent criticism directed at the Academy over the overrepresentation of Western white men among its picks.
There have been just 19 women laureates out of 122 since the Nobel literature prize was first awarded in 1901.
A 2018 sex assault scandal left the Academy in tatters and more than half of its 18 members were replaced.
Since then, every other literature laureate has been a woman.
Last year, the award went to Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai, whose works explore themes of postmodern dystopia.
The Nobel Prize comes with a diploma, a gold medal and a US$1.2 million (RM5 million) prize sum.
Carson will receive the award from King Carl XVI Gustaf in Stockholm on December 10, the anniversary of the 1896 death of scientist and prize creator Alfred Nobel. — AFP

d03c3c2c82317c9c: OCTOBER 8 — Another bullying case, another death and another number added to the statistics.
When tragedy is repeatedly reduced to numbers, there is a danger that society slowly becomes numb to it.
A child who dies after being bullied is not a statistic.
That child is someone's son or daughter, someone's friend and someone's student.
Behind every number is a family left to deal with a loss that no law, policy or government programme can ever reverse.
Malaysia has taken significant steps to address bullying.

The Anti-Bullying Act 2026 and Anti-Bullying Tribunal have strengthened the legal framework, while the government has expanded school safety measures, including CCTV coverage, additional hostel wardens, counselling and student protection initiatives.
Yet the scale of the problem remains worrying.
Ministry of Education data show that 7,681 bullying cases were recorded in schools in 2024, up from 6,528 in 2023.

More recently, the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2025 findings reported that 27 per cent of Malaysian students experienced at least one form of bullying several times a month or more, compared with 20 per cent across Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries.
These figures raise an uncomfortable question: What are we still missing?
Perhaps the missing piece is not another scheme, camera or regulation, but a deeper understanding of what happens before adults become aware of a problem.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

The Perlis Education Department said it won’t tolerate any form of bullying in educational institutions following an alleged incident involving a Form One student in Kangar that resulted in injuries. — Unsplash pic
A child who is bullied may fear retaliation, embarrassment or being labelled a “snitch”, while some may worry that reporting will make matters worse or that adults will not understand.
This is particularly difficult when the bully is part of the victim's own peer group.
A reporting system can only work if a frightened child trusts it enough to speak.
Parents therefore have an important role, but we cannot assume children will automatically explain what is happening.
Distress may instead appear through withdrawal, anxiety, reluctance to attend school, declining interest in studies, unexplained injuries or sudden changes in behaviour.
These signs do not necessarily mean bullying, but they should prompt adults to ask questions and listen carefully.
Schools also need to look beyond whether a policy exists on paper.
They must ensure that students know where to seek help, that complaints are taken seriously and that teachers have the confidence and support to escalate troubling patterns.
This does not mean blaming schools or teachers.
Rather, we should examine whether concerns about reputation, parental complaints or public scrutiny can sometimes make difficult cases harder to confront.
Experts have made a similar point.
Malaysian Mental Health Association president Andrew Mohanraj has argued that laws and tribunals need to be accompanied by a prevention-first approach involving schools, parents and digital safety.

Child protection specialist Lee Lyn Ni has likewise stressed that laws alone cannot solve bullying and that restorative approaches should help children understand the harm they cause and develop empathy.
This is why CCTV, wardens, counselling, laws and disciplinary measures, while necessary, cannot be the entire answer.
A camera can record an incident, but it cannot explain why a child was too frightened to report it.
A law can provide accountability, but it cannot remove the fear that prevents a victim from speaking.
We therefore need to understand the culture of silence surrounding bullying.
Why are victims afraid to speak?
Why do witnesses hesitate to intervene?
Why might parents miss the warning signs?
And could individual incidents sometimes be dismissed as minor disagreements when, collectively, they reveal a much more serious pattern?
Until we answer these questions, we risk adding more schemes without addressing the reasons bullying remains hidden.

The success of Malaysia's response should not be measured simply by the number of laws passed, cameras installed or programmes launched, but by whether a vulnerable child can speak, whether someone listens and whether that child is protected before the harm becomes irreversible.
A bullied child should never have to become another statistic before we realise that something has gone terribly wrong.
*The author is from the Department of Electrical, Electronic, and System Engineering, Faculty of Engineering and Built Environment, Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia.
* This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.

7764f44b1e0aa0cb: This week, we released our 2026 version of our Climate Tech Companies to Watch list. It’s an annual project that the MIT Technology Review team puts together. Our goal is to highlight some of the promising, interesting advances and firms we think are worth paying attention to in the world of climate and energy technology.

The list is always a little ray of hope for me—there are some fascinating ideas out there for changing how we power our world or moving away from fossil fuels to reduce the greenhouse-gas emissions that cause climate change.
Our chosen companies tend to reflect several aspects of the current moment. Here are some of the companies we picked and the key themes worth highlighting.
China is the center of the climate and energy tech world
Forgive me—I know I’ve made this point before. Feel free to call me Captain Obvious. But I think China’s dominance in energy technology is a global trend that bears repeated mentioning.

China is home to the world’s largest grid, and renewables are coming online more quickly than I can wrap my head around. Contributing to that boom is Envision Energy, a renewables giant appearing on our list for the second time. The company has installed over 100 gigawatts of wind power worldwide, as well as over 50 gigawatt-hours of battery storage.

Like many other Chinese companies right now, Envision is looking beyond the crowded Chinese market and setting its sights abroad, with projects in Germany, Brazil, and Australia and upcoming work in Vietnam.

China is also leading innovation in key technologies. I’ve been fascinated by the potential for next-generation batteries coming out of its companies: All the big ones, along with a host of smaller ones, are racing to develop solid-state batteries. They could be both safer than existing EV batteries and longer in range.

WeLion New Energy is particularly interesting. The battery company announced a big lab result last year, achieving 824 watt-hours per kilogram—more than three times the energy density of a standard lithium-ion battery today. Lab results in battery research are notoriously difficult to scale, but WeLion is also working to deploy semi-solid-state batteries, which could come to fruition faster than purely solid-state cells while still improving on lithium-ion’s performance.
Everybody wants a piece of the data center pie

We included just three companies from the US on the list, and two of them have received a major boost from Big Tech as companies look to power data centers. (The third, Brimstone, is leaning into another political hot topic, critical minerals.) Technologies that can provide consistent power are in high demand.

Fervo Energy is bringing next-generation geothermal power to the grid by using horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing to make it practical in more places. The company went public in May, raising $2.2 billion in its IPO, and plans to have a gigawatt’s worth of plants operational by the end of 2030.

X-energy is building helium-cooled small modular nuclear reactors. The reactors’ small size lends flexibility, and the company is currently working on a 320-megawatt cluster of them in collaboration with Amazon in Richland, Washington. (For what it’s worth, I’m interested in what this technology could do for industrial facilities—the company has a deal with Dow that could see it deployed at one of the company’s chemical plants in the early 2030s.)
The grid needs support, and energy storage will be a key piece moving forward

I know, I know—I haven’t stopped talking about batteries since I started writing this newsletter four years ago. But the energy storage market has surpassed even my expectations over that time. And as solar and wind quickly come online, they need storage to help them meet more of the grid’s demand.

Form Energy is on the list for a third time for its iron-air batteries, which could enable cheaper long-duration energy storage. The company has a massive project in the works, to the tune of 30 gigawatt-hours, which will be used to help power a Google data center. It could be the world’s largest battery project in terms of capacity by the time it comes online, which is expected to happen in phases between 2028 and 2031.

Taking another tack, Energy Dome is using compressed carbon dioxide to store energy on the grid. This technology is already cheaper than lithium-ion batteries for longer durations (think 10 hours or more), and the company is working to scale quickly. I covered the company in 2022, before it had its first commercial plant running. Now it has plans for over 30 gigawatt-hours’ worth of plants around the world, including one with Google in Ireland that’s slated to come online in 2028.

And Moment Energy is working to use the million EV batteries that are expected to reach the end of their life by 2030. The company has a facility in Vancouver, British Columbia, that repurposes used batteries for backup power.

This year hasn’t been all sunshine and rainbows for climate tech. But I’m hopeful that some of the companies on this list, and the technologies they build, will keep nudging us in the right direction.

fbff757ceb160117: The European Space Agency's Solar Orbiter has enabled scientists to trace magnetic switchbacks in the solar wind's magnetic field back to their source at the Sun. "Switchback" is the name given to an S-shaped kink in the solar wind's magnetic field – a sudden and large deflection. In 2022, the spacecraft gave scientists a full view of the structure (confirming the S-shape), but the origin remained up for debate. At the time, the probe's data suggested it might be near the Sun's surface, but a recent flight through a switchback allowed scientists to identify the source. "Solar Orbiter flew through a very large switchback," said Jesse Coburn of the French National Center for Scientific Research / Laboratoire de Phonétique et Phonologie (CNRS/LPP. "Because of this, we were able to sample rarely observed particles there that have tell-tale fingerprints of their origin." Solar Orbiter's Solar Wind Analyser instrument (SWA) was used to sample the switchback's plasma, and it came up with particles that could only have formed within hot magnetic loops at the surface of the Sun. Coburn said, "There are two main competing theories for how a switchback, and by extension the solar wind, forms. "The specific mix of particles detected by Solar Orbiter is the smoking gun for a formation process known as 'interchange reconnection'." This occurs when parts of the Sun with different magnetic properties interact. Some have field lines that stretch away into space. Others are closed and extend into space before looping back. When the two types meet, the lines can snap open, releasing previously trapped plasma into space. The other theory focuses on processes involving waves and turbulence. Stephanie Yardley of Northumbria University in the UK said, "Excitingly, we also see signs of these, but likely only after the switchback heads out into space. "Once the switchback has left the Sun, waves and turbulence take over and govern how it moves." Data from NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory was also stirred into the mix to reveal the switchback's solar source. It's exciting stuff and shows how the Sun heats its atmosphere and accelerates solar wind particles into space. It also has implications for predicting solar storms and their severity. Daniel Müller, ESA Project Scientist for Solar Orbiter, said, "As humans on Earth – and in space – our lives are entangled with what's happening on our star. The solar wind ties the Earth to the Sun, and our understanding of its dynamics has key implications for how we keep our planet safe from extreme space weather events. "The more we know, the better we can prepare for solar storms to protect our space-based infrastructure and technology." ®
